# Maintenance Report — MNT-0010-031

**Asset:** WELL-0010 (SW-23 Well 010, T350, Southwest Block 23)
**Equipment:** flowline
**Work started:** 08 Jan 2027 08:00 · **Finished:** 09 Jan 2027 02:00 · **Well stopped for this job:** 18 hours
**Crew lead:** Daniel Foster (U-302) · **Crew:** Kevin Price
**Triggered by:** inspection INS-0010-0218 on 2027-01-07
**Report written:** 10 Jan 2027

## What happened

The weekly manual inspection INS-0010-0218 at 08:45 on 2027-01-07 found crude oil on the pad: about 1.5% of the pad area, estimated 0.6 bbl. The inspector noted: "Pooled fluid near flowline." The field operator shut the well in, closed the flowline valve and placed earth berms and absorbent pads. The release was contained about 2.9 hours after the inspection. The crew traced the leak to a threaded coupling on the flowline close to the wellhead.

## Root cause

Corrosion under a failed protective wrap on the coupling.

## Safety and permits

- Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew before work started (WS-01).
- Energy isolated: prime mover stopped at the bottom of the stroke, brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged, wellhead wing valve closed and tagged, pressure bled off (WS-02).
- Personal H2S monitors worn; highest reading 0 ppm, below the 10 ppm stop-work level (WS-03).
- Hot work permit issued for welding; gas test before welding read 1% LEL, below the 10% limit (WS-04).

## Work done

1. Excavated around the coupling.
2. Cut out the failed coupling and the pipe ends.
3. Welded in new pipe and a new fitting.
4. Coated the new joints.
5. Excavated the stained soil.
6. Backfilled after the pressure test.

Summary of the fix: replaced leaking flowline section and remediated soil.

## Testing and return to service

Pressure-tested the repaired section at 226 psi (1.25 × the flowline's maximum operating pressure of 181 psi) and held it for 4 hours with no pressure drop (WS-05). The well was returned to production.

## Spill clean-up and waste

- About 0.5 m³ of stained soil excavated, bagged and sent to an approved disposal site under waste manifest WM-0010-031 (WS-06).
- 2 soil samples taken around the spill; the highest result after clean-up was 0.34% TPH, below the 1.0% target (SR-03).

**Triggered by:** inspection INS-0197-0212 on 2026-12-31
**Report written:** 15 Jan 2027 · **Status:** interim report, work still in progress

## What happened

Field staff reported that the operator noticed the pump jack running unusually light and no fluid reaching the flowline. The thermal reading at inspection INS-0197-0212 showed the wellhead at 9.8 °C with the air at 8.7 °C, so the well was not producing. The operator shut the well in for the repair. A dynamometer card showed no load from the downhole pump, which points to a parted rod.
The well is expected to stay shut in for about 16 days longer than the repair itself because the workover rig is busy on other wells.

## Root cause

A coupling unscrewed after repeated rod buckling at the bottom of the stroke.

## Safety and permits

- Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew before work started (WS-01).
- Energy isolated: prime mover stopped at the bottom of the stroke, brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged, wellhead wing valve closed and tagged, pressure bled off (WS-02).
- Personal H2S monitors worn; highest reading 8 ppm, below the 10 ppm stop-work level (WS-03).

## Work done so far

1. Rigged up the company workover rig on the well.
2. Pulled the rod string and located the break.

Still to do: complete the remaining repair steps, test the equipment and return the well to production.

Summary of the fix: fished and replaced parted rod section.

## Testing and return to service

Not done yet. The work is expected to finish on 19 Jan 2027; testing and return to service will be recorded in the final report.

# Maintenance Report — MNT-0175-033

**Asset:** WELL-0175 (NE-08 Well 175, T200, Northeast Block 8)
**Equipment:** flowline
**Work started:** 31 Jul 2026 08:00 · **Finished:** 01 Aug 2026 10:00 · **Well stopped for this job:** 26 hours
**Crew lead:** Kevin Price (U-303) · **Crew:** Megan Ward
**Triggered by:** inspection INS-0175-0193 on 2026-07-30
**Report written:** 01 Aug 2026

## What happened

The weekly drone inspection INS-0175-0193 at 11:45 on 2026-07-30 found crude oil on the pad: about 9.2% of the pad area, estimated 3.9 bbl. The inspector noted: "Dark staining on pad." The field operator shut the well in, closed the flowline valve and placed earth berms and absorbent pads. The release was contained about 2.8 hours after the inspection. The crew traced the leak to a threaded coupling on the flowline close to the wellhead.

## Root cause

Thread fatigue from pump jack vibration.

## Safety and permits

- Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew before work started (WS-01).
- Energy isolated: prime mover stopped at the bottom of the stroke, brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged, wellhead wing valve closed and tagged, pressure bled off (WS-02).
- Personal H2S monitors worn; highest reading 0 ppm, below the 10 ppm stop-work level (WS-03).
- Hot work permit issued for welding; gas test before welding read 0% LEL, below the 10% limit (WS-04).

## Work done

1. Excavated around the coupling.
2. Cut out the failed coupling and the pipe ends.
3. Welded in new pipe and a new fitting.
4. Coated the new joints.
5. Excavated the stained soil.
6. Backfilled after the pressure test.

Summary of the fix: replaced leaking flowline section and remediated soil.

## Testing and return to service

Pressure-tested the repaired section at 189 psi (1.25 × the flowline's maximum operating pressure of 151 psi) and held it for 4 hours with no pressure drop (WS-05). The well was returned to production.

## Spill clean-up and waste

- About 3.2 m³ of stained soil excavated, bagged and sent to an approved disposal site under waste manifest WM-0175-033 (WS-06).
- 2 soil samples taken around the spill; the highest result after clean-up was 0.72% TPH, below the 1.0% target (SR-03).
- Soil samples sent to the lab.

# Maintenance Report — MNT-0175-028

**Asset:** WELL-0175 (NE-08 Well 175, T200, Northeast Block 8)
**Equipment:** flowline
**Work started:** 06 Mar 2026 08:00 · **Finished:** 18 Mar 2026 12:00 · **Well stopped for this job:** 292 hours
**Crew lead:** Kevin Price (U-303) · **Crew:** Brian Coleman · **Contractor:** Tumbleweed Flowline Co.
**Triggered by:** inspection INS-0175-0173 on 2026-03-05
**Report written:** 20 Mar 2026

## What happened

Field staff reported that a damp, dark patch appeared along the flowline route. The thermal reading at inspection INS-0175-0173 showed the wellhead at 17.8 °C with the air at 15.7 °C, so the well was not producing. The operator shut the well in for the repair. Excavation found a corrosion pinhole on the bottom of the line.
The well stayed shut in for about 10 days longer than the repair itself because the replacement part was back-ordered from the supplier.

## Root cause

External corrosion where the pipe coating had been damaged.

## Safety and permits

- Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew before work started (WS-01).
- Energy isolated: prime mover stopped at the bottom of the stroke, brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged, wellhead wing valve closed and tagged, pressure bled off (WS-02).
- Personal H2S monitors worn; highest reading 3 ppm, below the 10 ppm stop-work level (WS-03).
- Hot work permit issued for welding; gas test before welding read 2% LEL, below the 10% limit (WS-04).

## Work done

1. Excavated around the leak.
2. Cut out the corroded section.
3. Welded in a new section of line pipe.
4. Coated the new joint.
5. Backfilled after the pressure test.

Summary of the fix: cut out and replaced the corroded flowline section.

## Testing and return to service

Pressure-tested the repaired section at 189 psi (1.25 × the flowline's maximum operating pressure of 151 psi) and held it for 4 hours with no pressure drop (WS-05). The well was returned to production.

## Waste

- Oily soil from the excavation and the cut-out pipe sent to an approved disposal site under waste manifest WM-0175-028 (WS-06).

## Parts and cost

| Line pipe section | 1,849 |
| Welding consumables and coating | 1,109 |
| Excavation services | 740 |
| Labour (company crew and contractor) | 3,463 |
| **Total** | **7,161** |

## Compliance check

| Protocol | Result | Detail |

| WS-01 | Met | Meeting held and recorded |
| WS-02 | Met | Energy isolated and tagged |
| WS-03 | Met | Monitors bump-tested; highest 3 ppm |
| WS-04 | Met | Permit issued; gas test 2% LEL |
| WS-05 | Met | Tested at 1.25 × maximum operating pressure, held 4 hours |
| WS-06 | Met | Oily waste manifested to an approved site |
| WS-07 | Met | Written 2 days after the work (limit 3 days) |

## Notes and recommendations

- Check wall thickness along the rest of this flowline.
- Consider corrosion inhibitor injection.

# Maintenance Report — MNT-0197-022

**Asset:** WELL-0197 (NE-08 Well 197, T200, Northeast Block 8)
**Equipment:** pump jack
**Work started:** 28 Dec 2025 08:00 · **Finished:** 20 Jan 2026 04:00 · **Well stopped for this job:** 548 hours
**Crew lead:** Kevin Price (U-303) · **Crew:** Daniel Foster
**Triggered by:** inspection INS-0197-0160 on 2025-12-25
**Report written:** 21 Jan 2026

## What happened

Field staff reported that the pump jack was running rough with a loud knock at the top of each stroke, so the operator stopped it. The thermal reading at inspection INS-0197-0160 showed the wellhead at 10.7 °C with the air at 7.5 °C, so the well was not producing. The operator shut the well in for the repair. A vibration check and visual inspection found play in the saddle bearing and scoring on the bearing housing.
The well stayed shut in for about 21 days longer than the repair itself because the crew was committed to a higher-priority spill response elsewhere in the field.

## Root cause

Grease contaminated with sand had worn the bearing.

## Safety and permits

- Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew before work started (WS-01).
- Energy isolated: prime mover stopped at the bottom of the stroke, brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged, wellhead wing valve closed and tagged, pressure bled off (WS-02).

## Work done

1. Lowered the horsehead and supported the walking beam with a crane.
2. Removed the saddle bearing assembly.
3. Cleaned the housing and checked alignment.
4. Fitted a new saddle bearing and torqued the bolts to the manufacturer's values.
5. Greased all structural bearings.

Summary of the fix: replaced saddle bearing and re-greased.

## Testing and return to service

Ran the unit for 2 hours: smooth stroke, no knocking, bearing temperature normal. The well was returned to production.

# Maintenance Report — MNT-0010-020

**Asset:** WELL-0010 (SW-23 Well 010, T200, Southwest Block 23)
**Equipment:** flowline
**Work started:** 08 Aug 2025 08:00 · **Finished:** 09 Aug 2025 08:00 · **Well stopped for this job:** 24 hours
**Crew lead:** Megan Ward (U-305) · **Crew:** Daniel Foster, Kevin Price · **Contractor:** Tumbleweed Flowline Co.
**Triggered by:** inspection INS-0010-0144 on 2025-08-07
**Report written:** 10 Aug 2025

## What happened

The weekly drone inspection INS-0010-0144 at 15:30 on 2025-08-07 found crude oil on the pad: about 8.7% of the pad area, estimated 2.7 bbl. The inspector noted: "Dark staining on pad." The field operator shut the well in, closed the flowline valve and placed earth berms and absorbent pads. The release was contained about 2.4 hours after the inspection. The crew traced the leak to a threaded coupling on the flowline close to the wellhead.

## Root cause

Thread fatigue from pump jack vibration.

## Safety and permits

- Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew before work started (WS-01).
- Energy isolated: prime mover stopped at the bottom of the stroke, brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged, wellhead wing valve closed and tagged, pressure bled off (WS-02).

- Hot work permit issued for welding; gas test before welding read 3% LEL, below the 10% limit (WS-04).

## Work done

1. Excavated around the coupling.
2. Cut out the failed coupling and the pipe ends.
3. Welded in new pipe and a new fitting.
4. Coated the new joints.
5. Excavated the stained soil.
6. Backfilled after the pressure test.

Summary of the fix: replaced leaking flowline section and remediated soil.

## Testing and return to service

Pressure-tested the repaired section at 226 psi (1.25 × the flowline's maximum operating pressure of 181 psi) and held it for 4 hours with no pressure drop (WS-05). The well was returned to production.

## Spill clean-up and waste

- About 3.0 m³ of stained soil excavated, bagged and sent to an approved disposal site under waste manifest WM-0010-020 (WS-06).
- 2 soil samples taken around the spill; the highest result after clean-up was 0.59% TPH, below the 1.0% target (SR-03).

# Maintenance Report — MNT-0197-020

**Asset:** WELL-0197 (NE-08 Well 197, T200, Northeast Block 8)
**Equipment:** pump jack
**Work started:** 04 Jul 2025 08:00 · **Finished:** 30 Jul 2025 17:00 · **Well stopped for this job:** 633 hours
**Crew lead:** Brian Coleman (U-304) · **Crew:** Megan Ward · **Contractor:** Coyote Ridge Well Services
**Triggered by:** inspection INS-0197-0137 on 2025-07-03
**Report written:** 30 Jul 2025

## What happened

Field staff reported that oil was dripping from the gearbox onto the pump jack base. The thermal reading at inspection INS-0197-0137 showed the wellhead at 35.2 °C with the air at 32.9 °C, so the well was not producing. The operator shut the well in for the repair. The input shaft seal was worn and the gearbox oil level was below the sight glass.
The well stayed shut in for about 24 days longer than the repair itself because the job had to wait for a weekday contractor slot.

## Root cause

# Maintenance Report — MNT-0197-004

**Asset:** WELL-0197 (NE-08 Well 197, T200, Northeast Block 8)
**Equipment:** flowline
**Work started:** 02 Apr 2023 08:00 · **Finished:** 11 Apr 2023 16:00 · **Well stopped for this job:** 224 hours
**Crew lead:** Daniel Foster (U-302) · **Crew:** Megan Ward, Kevin Price · **Contractor:** Tumbleweed Flowline Co.
**Triggered by:** inspection INS-0197-0024 on 2023-03-30
**Report written:** 12 Apr 2023

## What happened

Field staff reported that the inspector saw wet soil above the buried flowline. The thermal reading at inspection INS-0197-0024 showed the wellhead at 18.6 °C with the air at 15.9 °C, so the well was not producing. The operator shut the well in for the repair. Excavation found a corrosion pinhole on the bottom of the line.
The well stayed shut in for about 7 days longer than the repair itself because heavy rain made the lease road impassable for the service truck.

## Root cause

External corrosion where the pipe coating had been damaged.

## Safety and permits

- Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew before work started (WS-01).
- Energy isolated: prime mover stopped at the bottom of the stroke, brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged, wellhead wing valve closed and tagged, pressure bled off (WS-02).
- Personal H2S monitors worn; highest reading 6 ppm, below the 10 ppm stop-work level (WS-03).
- Hot work permit issued for welding; gas test before welding read 0% LEL, below the 10% limit (WS-04).

## Work done

1. Excavated around the leak.
2. Cut out the corroded section.
3. Welded in a new section of line pipe.
4. Coated the new joint.
5. Backfilled after the pressure test.

Summary of the fix: cut out and replaced the corroded flowline section.

## Testing and return to service

Pressure-tested the repaired section at 244 psi (1.25 × the flowline's maximum operating pressure of 195 psi) and held it for 4 hours with no pressure drop (WS-05). The well was returned to production.

## Waste

- Oily soil from the excavation and the cut-out pipe sent to an approved disposal site under waste manifest WM-0197-004 (WS-06).

## Parts and cost

| Item | USD |
|---|---|
| Line pipe section | 1,795 |
| Welding consumables and coating | 1,077 |
| Excavation services | 718 |
| Labour (company crew and contractor) | 1,610 |
| **Total** | **5,200** |

## Compliance check

| Protocol | Result | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| WS-01 | Met | Meeting held and recorded |
| WS-02 | Met | Energy isolated and tagged |
| WS-03 | Met | Monitors bump-tested; highest 6 ppm |
| WS-04 | Met | Permit issued; gas test 0% LEL |
| WS-05 | Met | Tested at 1.25 × maximum operating pressure, held 4 hours |
| WS-06 | Met | Oily waste manifested to an approved site |
| WS-07 | Met | Written 1 day after the work (limit 3 days) |

## Notes and recommendations

- Check wall thickness along the rest of this flowline.
- Consider corrosion inhibitor injection.

# Maintenance Report — MNT-0197-001

**Asset:** WELL-0197 (NE-08 Well 197, T200, Northeast Block 8)
**Equipment:** rod string
**Work started:** 04 Dec 2022 08:00 · **Finished:** 07 Dec 2022 04:00 · **Well stopped for this job:** 68 hours
**Crew lead:** Kevin Price (U-303) · **Crew:** Daniel Foster
**Triggered by:** inspection INS-0197-0007 on 2022-12-01
**Report written:** 08 Dec 2022

## What happened

Field staff reported that the pump jack was running but the wellhead was cold and the rod load had dropped. The thermal reading at inspection INS-0197-0007 showed the wellhead at 16.6 °C with the air at 13.6 °C, so the well was not producing. The operator shut the well in for the repair. A dynamometer card showed no load from the downhole pump, which points to a parted rod.

## Root cause

A coupling unscrewed after repeated rod buckling at the bottom of the stroke.

## Safety and permits

3. Recovered the lower section with an overshot fishing tool.
4. Replaced the damaged rods.
5. Ran the rod string back in and spaced out the pump.

Summary of the fix: fished and replaced parted rod section.

## Testing and return to service

Pump test showed normal fluid delivery and the rod load returned to normal. The well was returned to production.

The weekly drone inspection INS-0175-0005 at 10:30 on 2022-11-17 found crude oil on the pad: about 2.2% of the pad area, estimated 1.3 bbl. The inspector noted: "Oil sheen around cellar." The field operator shut the well in, closed the flowline valve and placed earth berms and absorbent pads. The release was contained about 3.0 hours after the inspection. # T200 Rod-Lift Oil Well — Operating & Maintenance Manual

> Fictional manual written for the FlytBase Asset Copilot hackathon. Modelled on typical
> sucker-rod (beam pump) well practice. Not for real-world operational use.

Document ID: OM-T200 · Revision 4 · Applies to all wells with `well_type = "T200"`

## 1. Scope

This manual covers the T200 class of onshore rod-lift (beam pump) oil wells: a
conventional wellhead, a surface pump jack (walking-beam pumping unit), a sucker
rod string, an insert downhole pump and a 3-inch carbon-steel flowline to the
area gathering line. Some T200 pads also carry a two-phase vertical separator.

## 2. Equipment overview

| Equipment | Typical model | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Wellhead | WH-3000 | Seals the well, holds the stuffing box and production valves |
| Pump jack | PJ-228 | Converts motor rotation to reciprocating rod motion |
| Rod string | API Grade D 7/8 in | Transmits motion from the pump jack to the downhole pump |
| Downhole pump | Insert rod pump 1.75 in | Lifts fluid from the reservoir |
| Flowline | 3 in carbon steel | Carries produced fluid to the gathering line |
| Separator (optional) | 2-phase vertical 24 in | Separates gas from liquid on the pad |

## 3. Normal operation

A producing T200 well cycles continuously at 6–9 strokes per minute. Produced
fluid leaves the reservoir warmer than the surface air, so a producing wellhead
runs noticeably warmer than ambient. When the pump stops, the
wellhead cools to near ambient within a few hours.

Operators should expect daily and seasonal variation. On hot summer afternoons
the steel of an idle wellhead can read well above 45 °C from solar heating alone.
**Never judge production from absolute wellhead temperature.**

## 4. Start-up and shut-in

1. Confirm the flowline valve is open and the separator (if fitted) is at operating level.
2. Release the pump jack brake and start the prime mover.
3. Confirm stroke rate within 6–9 spm and check the stuffing box for leaks.
4. For a planned shut-in, stop the prime mover at the bottom of the stroke, set the brake,
   close the wing valve and record the shut-in in the maintenance system before work starts.

## 5. Routine inspection checklist

- Visual check of pad, cellar and flowline route for staining or pooled fluid.
- Thermal reading of the wellhead (drone or handheld).
- Stuffing box leakage, belt condition and gearbox oil level.
- Separator level and dump valve operation (if fitted).

## 6. Lubrication schedule

| Item | Interval |
|---|---|
| Saddle and tail bearings | 90 days |
| Gearbox oil level check | 30 days |
| Gearbox oil change | 12 months |
| Belt tension | 60 days |

## 7. Common failure modes

| Symptom | Likely cause | First action |
|---|---|---|
| Unit running, wellhead cold | Rod parted or pump stuck | Shut in, call rod/pump crew |
| Unit stopped, motor hot | Prime mover overload | Reset overload, check cooling |
| Oil on gearbox base | Seal failure | Replace seals |
| Staining along flowline | Corrosion pinhole or coupling failure | Shut in, contain, report per SOP SR |
| Stuffing box weeping | Worn packing | Replace packing |

## 8. Spill response on the pad

Any crude release must be handled under the company Spill Response SOP
(`sops/spill-response-sop.md`). In short: stop the source, contain, estimate the
volume, and report within the deadline set by the SOP.

## 9. Engineering limits

### 9.1 Pressure
Maximum allowable wellhead working pressure: 3,000 psi.

### 9.2 Stroke
Maximum stroke rate: 10 spm. Maximum polished-rod load: 22,800 lb.

### 9.3 Production temperature rule
A T200 well is considered **producing (active)** when its wellhead temperature is
at least **15 °C above ambient** air temperature at the time of the reading. A
difference below 15 °C means the well is **not producing** for that reading,
whatever the absolute temperature.

### 9.4 Temperature alarm
The wellhead must stay **at or below 85 °C**. Any reading above 85 °C requires the
operator to shut in and inspect the stuffing box and rod string within 24 hours.

### 9.5 Spill-related shut-in
If a spill covers **more than 5 % of the pad area**, shut in the well immediately and
keep it shut in until the source is repaired.

## 10. Maintenance escalation

- Three or more **corrective** maintenance events on the same equipment kind in the
  12 months before the current date require a root-cause analysis (RCA) before the next repair is closed.
- Downtime of more than 14 consecutive days must be reported to the area production supervisor.
- An annual flowline integrity test is mandatory (see Regulatory Compliance SOP, RC-02).

## 11. Records

Every inspection, maintenance job and shut-in must be recorded. Human notes that
explain an abnormal reading (for example a planned shut-in) are valid context and
should be considered alongside the sensor data.

# T350 Deep Rod-Lift Oil Well — Operating & Maintenance Manual

> Fictional manual written for the FlytBase Asset Copilot hackathon. Not for real-world use.

Document ID: OM-T350 · Revision 2 · Applies to all wells with `well_type = "T350"`

## 1. Scope

The T350 is a deeper, higher-rate version of the T200 rod-lift well. It uses a
WH-5000 wellhead, a PJ-456 pump jack and the same rod, pump and
flowline families as the T200. Procedures not listed here follow the T200 manual.

## 2. Differences from T200

| Item | T200 | T350 |
|---|---|---|
| Wellhead rating | 3,000 psi | 5,000 psi |
| Pump jack | PJ-228 | PJ-456 |
| Normal stroke rate | 6–9 spm | 5–8 spm |
| Max polished-rod load | 22,800 lb | 45,600 lb |

## 3. Production temperature rule

Because T350 fluid comes from a deeper, hotter zone, a T350 well is considered
**producing (active)** only when its wellhead temperature is at least **20 °C above
ambient** air temperature at the time of the reading.

## 4. Temperature alarm

The wellhead must stay **at or below 95 °C**. Above 95 °C, shut in and inspect within 24 hours.

## 5. Spill-related shut-in

Same as T200: a spill covering more than 5 % of the pad area requires immediate shut-in.

## 6. Maintenance escalation

Same as T200 section 10 (RCA after three corrective events on the same equipment
kind within 12 months; report downtime over 14 consecutive days).

# T500 Electric Submersible Pump Oil Well — Operating & Maintenance Manual

> Fictional manual written for the FlytBase Asset Copilot hackathon. Modelled on typical
> electric submersible pump (ESP) well practice. Not for real-world operational use.

Document ID: OM-T500 · Revision 1 · Applies to all wells with `well_type = "T500"`

## 1. Scope

The T500 is a high-rate well lifted by an **electric submersible pump (ESP)** instead of a
pump jack and rod string. There is no surface pumping unit: a variable-speed drive on the
pad powers a motor and multistage pump hung on the tubing deep in the well. The wellhead,
flowline and optional separator are the same families as on rod-lift wells.

## 2. Equipment overview

| Equipment | Typical model | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Wellhead | WH-5000 | Seals the well, carries the power cable penetrator and production valves |
| ESP (`esp_pump`) | ESP-400 | Downhole motor, seal section and multistage pump, with its surface drive and power cable |
| Flowline | 3 in carbon steel | Carries produced fluid to the gathering line |
| Separator (optional) | 2-phase vertical 24 in | Separates gas from liquid on the pad |

A T500 pad has **no pump jack, rod string or rod pump**. There is no visible stroke, so a
drone cannot tell from movement alone whether the well is running.

## 3. Production temperature rule

ESP wells move more fluid, and the motor adds heat. A T500 well is considered
**producing (active)** only when its wellhead temperature is at least **25 °C above
ambient** air temperature at the time of the reading. Below 25 °C the well is **not
producing** for that reading.

## 4. Temperature alarm

The wellhead must stay **at or below 95 °C**. Above 95 °C, shut in and check the drive
and motor within 24 hours.

## 5. Early warning signs

An ESP runs at a steady speed, so a healthy T500 wellhead stays within a degree or two of
its usual difference above air. ESP motors usually fail after running hot with too little
fluid over the pump. In the weeks before a failure, the wellhead-to-air difference typically
**falls steadily** while the well is still producing.

- If the wellhead-to-air difference is **lower than at the inspection before, three
  inspections in a row** (four readings, each lower than the last) **and has fallen by
  3 °C or more in total** over those four readings, schedule an ESP drive and insulation
  check within **14 days** of the third drop.
- A ground fault or repeated trips on the drive must be treated as a failure, not reset.

## 6. Spill-related shut-in

Same as T200: a spill covering more than 5 % of the pad area requires immediate shut-in.

## 7. Maintenance escalation

- **Two or more** corrective maintenance events on the **ESP** in the 12 months before the
  current date require a root-cause analysis (RCA) before the next repair is closed.
  (ESP pulls need a workover rig and cost far more than rod-lift repairs.)
- For all other equipment, follow T200 section 10 (three events in 12 months).
- Downtime of more than 14 consecutive days must be reported to the area production supervisor.
- An annual flowline integrity test is mandatory (see Regulatory Compliance SOP, RC-02).

chunk_be79f781cbf9405bf13bdab3.title: What happened
chunk_be79f781cbf9405bf13bdab3.excerpt:
Field staff reported that the separator high-level alarm stayed on. The thermal reading at inspection INS-0010-0172 showed the wellhead at 17.3 °C with the air at 13.9 °C, so the well was not producing. The operator shut the well in for the repair. The level controller had failed.
The well stayed shut in for about 2 days longer than the repair itself because the replacement part was back-ordered from the supplier.

chunk_ec7c67cf84bac30467375684.title: What happened
chunk_ec7c67cf84bac30467375684.excerpt:
Field staff reported that the motor breaker kept tripping and the pump jack would not run. The thermal reading at inspection INS-0010-0183 showed the wellhead at 29.3 °C with the air at 23.7 °C, so the well was not producing. The operator shut the well in for the repair. An insulation test showed a winding fault, so the motor was replaced with an exchange unit.
The well stayed shut in for about 2 days longer than the repair itself because the job had to wait for a weekday contractor slot.

chunk_40b41d47e1c00491a32fccc2.title: What happened
chunk_40b41d47e1c00491a32fccc2.excerpt:
Field staff reported that the electric motor driving the pump jack had stopped and would not restart. The thermal reading at inspection INS-0010-0094 showed the wellhead at 40.0 °C with the air at 35.0 °C, so the well was not producing. The operator shut the well in for the repair. An insulation test showed a winding fault, so the motor was replaced with an exchange unit.
The well stayed shut in for about 2 days longer than the repair itself because the job had to wait for a weekday contractor slot.

chunk_6e093fb9670b5f753035638c.title: Testing and return to service
chunk_6e093fb9670b5f753035638c.excerpt: Pressure-tested the repaired section at 226 psi (1.25 × the flowline's maximum operating pressure of 181 psi) and held it for 4 hours with no pressure drop (WS-05). The well was returned to production.
